title: LinkedIn games analysis pipeline
text:
← Projects
This is a personal project to create a live analysis pipeline that will show descriptive analysis of daily LinkedIn games records between PM and CW.
This pipeline will serve to elucidate who is the better overall player in LinkedIn games (Tango, Zip, Pinpoint and Cross climb) to date; between players PM and CW. Beginning from April 29th till today, August 13, 2026, data will continually be updated manually in the raw .xlsx file and ran through the pipeline for analysis when rendered.
In addition to summarizing means, medians, standard deviations, and visualizing score distributions over time, this document also employs Bayesian independent‐samples t‐tests for each game type to quantify the strength of evidence for performance differences between PM and CW. In each case, Bayes factors (BF10) is computed along with prior and posterior distributions plotted to illustrate how observed data update our beliefs about any effect (see Note 1 below).
This document aims to describe, visualize, and evaluate, using both descriptive statistics and Bayesian hypothesis tests, to assess the differences in scores between the two players.
# Libraries utilized
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(car)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(BayesFactor)

# Load the data in
dat <- read_xlsx("LinkedIn_games_data.xlsx")
To account for missing data (e.g., failure to complete Pinpoint guesses), “-” will be recoded into N.A. and listwise deletion will be conducted to remove the data for the day. Additionally, since the data is manually entered, it is recorded in wide format. The code below pivots the wide format into long format, which is simpler for analysis.
Show the code
# Convert "-" into NA and all columns into double
dat <- dat %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(., "-"))) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.double)) 

# Change to long format
dat_long <- dat %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = c("Player", "Game_type"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "value"
  )

Descriptive statistics
This section summarizes the central tendencies and variability in the players’ daily game performance across the four game types (Tango (T), Zip(Z), Pinpoint(P), and Crossclimb(C)), using standard measures of mean, median and standard deviation.


Show the code
# Calculate mean, median and SD for understanding average
summary_stats <- dat_long %>% 
  group_by(Player, Game_type) %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Median = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Standard_Deviation = round(sd(value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Store central tendencies scores for inline updating
## Tango (Mean)
mean_t_PM <- summary_stats %>%
  filter(Game_type == "T", Player == "PM") %>%
  pull(Mean)
mean_t_CW <- summary_stats %>%
  filter(Game_type == "T", Player == "CW") %>%
  pull(Mean)
## Zip (Mean)

Time-series visualizations
The time‐series plots display each player’s daily performance (e.g., completion time (seconds) or number of tries) on the x‐axis (date) and the corresponding score on the y‐axis.
These visualizations provide comparisons of variability and stability to assess player score fluctuations and identify any days with unusually high or low values (and identify and potential outliers). It provides an intuitive and chronological overview of how PM and CW’s LinkedIn game scores evolve.
The data is first subset into the four game type prior to visualizations.

title: LinkedIn games analysis pipeline
text:
Bayesian Independent T-test comparisons
Here, using Bayesian Independent-samples t-tests, evidence for or against a difference in performance between PM and CW for each game type will be quantified. For each comparison, the Bayes factor (BF10) ia computed to measure the relative support for the alternative hypothesis (that the two players differ in average game scores) over the null hypothesis (no difference).
Additionally, prior (default) and posterior distributions of the standardized effect size will be calculated to assess how the observed data update beliefs under the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)






Note 1: IMPORTANT NOTE



The subsequent analysis is made purely for fun. This is not a formalized statistics project, and even though Bayesian analysis is more robust to optional-stopping than frequentist methods, there are important considerations.

Continously re-running the analysis with the same default prior (Cauchy scale = 0.707) without formally updating it in light of past data can produce Bayes factors that are not strictly coherent under sequential updating.
Proper sequential analysis would require recalculating the posterior at each stage and using that as the new prior for the next stage. Here, the analysis always begins from the default prior, which may under or overestimate evidence until enough data have accumulated. Each Bayes Factor value should be regarded as snapshots of a formal sequentially updated analysis.

These results can only be used as informal visualization and intuitive understanding rather than confirmatory statistical proof.



Homogenity of Variance Assumptions
Runs Levene’s test as a check of homogenity of variance for each game type subsets. Although Bayesian t‐tests are typically robust to mild heterogeneity of variance, it remains good practice to understand whether this assumption might be violated.

TangoZipPinpointCrossclimb




Show the code
# Levene's test of homogenity of variance
levene_T <- leveneTest(value ~ as.factor(Player), data = dat_longT)
levene_T_df <- as.data.frame(levene_T)

# Clean up df formatting
levene_T_df <- levene_T_df %>% 
  mutate(
    `Df` = Df,
    `F Value` = round(`F value`, 3),
    `Pr(>F)` = signif(`Pr(>F)`, 3)
  ) %>% 
  select(`Df`, `F Value`, `Pr(>F)`)

# Create Clean table
levene_T_df %>% 
  kable(
    caption = "Levene’s Test for Homogeneity of Variance",
    col.names = c("Degrees of Freedom", "F Statistic", "p-value"),
    format = "html"
  ) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center", bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

Bayes Factor computation

TangoZipPinpointCrossclimb


Bayes factor computation for Tango between PM and CW.


Show the code
# Filter out PM’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_pm <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "PM", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Filter out CW’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_cw <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "CW", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Run Bayesian two-sample t-test
bf_obj_tango <- ttestBF(
  x = tango_pm,
  y = tango_cw,
  paired = FALSE
)

# extractBF() returns a data frame; the “bf” column is the numeric Bayes Factor
bf_tango <- extractBF(bf_obj_tango)$bf[1]

# Build a simple one‐row data.frame for kable()
data.frame(
  "Game Type" = "Tango",
  "BF10"      = round(bf_tango, 3),
  "Notes"     = if (bf_tango > 1) {
                   "Evidence favoring difference (H1)"
                 } else {
                   "Evidence favoring H0 or inconclusive"
                 }
) %>%
  # Display as HTML table with caption and styling
  kable(
    caption   = "Bayesian independent‐samples t‐test (Tango)",
    col.names = c("Game Type", "BF₁₀", "Notes"),
    format    = "html"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width        = FALSE,
    position          = "center",
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")
  )

Visualizations of posterior and prior distributions.


Show the code
# Obtain 10,000 posterior samples of the standardized effect size (delta)
posterior_samples_T <- posterior(bf_obj_tango, iterations = 10000)

# Convert to a data frame for easier handling
posterior_df_T <- as.data.frame(posterior_samples_T)

# Create a sequence of effect size (delta) values for the prior
delta_range_T <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)  # reasonable range for visualization

# Compute the density of the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)
prior_density_T <- dcauchy(delta_range_T, location = 0, scale = sqrt(2) / 2)

# Create a data frame for the prior distribution
prior_df_T <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range_T,
  density = prior_density_T,
  Distribution = "Prior"
)

# Compute the density of the posterior samples
posterior_density_T <- density(posterior_df_T$delta, adjust = 1.5)  # adjust can be tuned for smoothing

posterior_df_density_T <- data.frame(
  delta = posterior_density_T$x,
  density = posterior_density_T$y,
  Distribution = "Posterior"
)

# Combine prior and posterior data frames
combined_df_T <- rbind(prior_df_T, posterior_df_density_T)

# Plot both distributions
ggplot(combined_df_T, aes(x = delta, y = density, color = Distribution, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.2, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior and Posterior Distributions of Effect Size (δ)",
    subtitle = "Tango: PM vs. CW",
    x = "Effect Size (δ)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

posterior_df_pp <- as.data.frame(posterior_samples_pp)

# Create a sequence of effect size (delta) values for the prior
delta_range_pp <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)  # reasonable range for visualization

# Compute the density of the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)
prior_density_pp <- dcauchy(delta_range_pp, location = 0, scale = sqrt(2) / 2)

# Create a data frame for the prior distribution
prior_df_pp <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range_pp,
  density = prior_density_pp,
  Distribution = "Prior"
)

# Compute the density of the posterior samples
posterior_density_pp <- density(posterior_df_pp$delta, adjust = 1.5)  # adjust can be tuned for smoothing

posterior_df_density_pp <- data.frame(
  delta = posterior_density_pp$x,
  density = posterior_density_pp$y,
  Distribution = "Posterior"
)

# Combine prior and posterior data frames
combined_df_pp <- rbind(prior_df_pp, posterior_df_density_pp)

# Plot both distributions
ggplot(combined_df_pp, aes(x = delta, y = density, color = Distribution, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.2, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior and Posterior Distributions of Effect Size (δ)",
    subtitle = "Pinpoint: PM vs. CW",
    x = "Effect Size (δ)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
This document demonstrates a complete Bayesian analysis pipeline in R for a simple reaction time experiment with a 2×2 factorial design. The goal is to show, in a clear and reproducible way, how to move from a simulated dataset to a fitted Bayesian mixed-effects model, and then on to interpretation of the posterior, predictions, and basic hypothesis tests.
The focus here is practical. I assume you are comfortable with basic R, regression-type models, and the idea of random effects, but perhaps newer to Bayesian modelling with brms. Throughout, I explain the key Bayesian concepts that are directly relevant to the workflow, including priors, posterior distributions, mixed-effects modelling, and MCMC sampling.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Experimental Scenario
The example is grounded in a cognitive psychology setting. Imagine an experiment where participants respond to visual targets while two experimental factors are manipulated. The first factor is Viewing Condition, where participants either have a Restricted view or an Unrestricted view of some relevant aspect of the display. The second factor is Target Location, which can be Same or Different relative to a previous location.
The outcome of interest is reaction time (RT) in milliseconds. In line with typical inhibition-of-return paradigms, the data are simulated so that responses are slower when the target appears in the same location compared to a different one. The expected inhibition effect is around 20–30 ms. Viewing condition is not expected to have a strong effect, and there is no strong interaction between viewing condition and target location.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Setup and Data Generation
To begin, I load the necessary packages and set a seed for reproducibility. The main packages used are tidyverse for data handling, brms for the Bayesian modelling, bayestestR and bayesplot for working with the posterior, and tidybayes for tidy posterior extraction.

library(tidyverse) # Data wrangling and visualisation
library(brms) # Bayesian regression models (Stan backend)
library(bayestestR) # Posterior summaries and hypothesis tests
library(bayesplot) # Posterior visualisation tools
library(tidybayes) # Tidy extraction of posterior samples

set.seed(42)

Next, I create a trial-level dataset that reflects the 2×2 design and the expected pattern of means. 30 participants complete 24 trials per condition, producing a reasonably sized data set to resemble a modest laboratory sample.

# Parameters for simulation
n_subj   <- 30          # Number of participants
n_trials <- 24          # Trials per condition per participant

# Define cell means (ms), one row per condition so there's no risk of the
# means lining up with the wrong condition (expand.grid()'s row order isn't
# always what you'd guess - listing conditions explicitly avoids that trap)
# These values encode a ~25 ms inhibition effect for "Same" vs. "Different"
mu_table <- tribble(
  ~Viewing,       ~Location,    ~mean, ~sd,
  "Restricted",   "Same",         530,  30,
  "Restricted",   "Different",    505,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Same",         525,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Different",    500,  30
)

# Generate trial-level data
dat <- expand.grid(
  Subj     = 1:n_subj,
  Viewing  = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted"),
  Location = c("Same", "Different"),
  Trial    = 1:n_trials
) %>%
  left_join(mu_table, by = c("Viewing", "Location")) %>%
  mutate(
    RT      = rnorm(n(), mean = mean, sd = sd),
    Subj    = factor(Subj),
    Viewing = factor(Viewing, levels = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted")),
    Location = factor(Location, levels = c("Different", "Same"))
  ) %>%
  select(Subj, Viewing, Location, Trial, RT)

head(dat, 12)

   Subj    Viewing Location Trial       RT
1     1 Restricted     Same     1 571.1288
2     2 Restricted     Same     1 513.0591
3     3 Restricted     Same     1 540.8939
4     4 Restricted     Same     1 548.9859
5     5 Restricted     Same     1 542.1280
6     6 Restricted     Same     1 526.8163

8     8 Restricted     Same     1 527.1602
9     9 Restricted     Same     1 590.5527
10   10 Restricted     Same     1 528.1186
11   11 Restricted     Same     1 569.1461
12   12 Restricted     Same     1 598.5994


At this point, I briefly check that the simulation behaves as intended. The condition means should show longer RTs in the Same condition than in the Different condition, with only small differences between viewing conditions.

dat %>%
  group_by(Viewing, Location) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_RT = mean(RT),
    sd_RT   = sd(RT),
    n       = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Viewing      Location  mean_RT sd_RT     n
  <fct>        <fct>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 Restricted   Different    504.  28.3   720
2 Restricted   Same         530.  31.0   720
3 Unrestricted Different    499.  30.3   720
4 Unrestricted Same         526.  30.6   720


This simple summary reassures us that the simulated dataset captures the qualitative pattern we designed.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Priors
Before fitting, it’s worth being explicit about the priors. brms will pick default (flat or very weakly informative) priors automatically, but a Bayesian workflow is more transparent when priors are chosen deliberately. Here I use weakly informative priors centred on plausible values given the scale of the data (reaction times in the 400-600ms range, with an expected effect of a few tens of milliseconds):

Intercept: normal(500, 100) - centred on a plausible average RT, wide enough to not rule out much.
Fixed-effect coefficients (b): normal(0, 50) - centred on “no effect”, allowing effects up to roughly +/-100ms to be plausible a priori.
Residual and random-intercept SDs: exponential(1) - a standard weakly informative choice for scale parameters, keeping them positive and not too large.


priors <- c(
  prior(normal(500, 100), class = Intercept),
  prior(normal(0, 50),   class = b),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sigma),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sd)
)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Model fit

fit <- brm(
  formula = RT ~ Viewing * Location + (1 | Subj),
  data    = dat,
  family  = gaussian(),
  prior   = priors,
  chains  = 4,
  cores   = 4,
  iter    = 2000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  seed    = 42,
  backend = "rstan"
)

chains = 4 runs four independent MCMC chains so we can check they agree with each other (a key diagnostic for whether sampling has worked properly). warmup = 1000 discards the first 1000 iterations per chain while the sampler tunes itself, keeping the remaining 1000 per chain (4000 total) as usable posterior draws.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
MCMC diagnostics
Before trusting any of the results, we check that the chains converged. Rhat values close to 1.00 indicate the chains agree with each other, and Bulk_ESS/Tail_ESS indicate how many effectively independent draws we have.

summary(fit)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Posterior summaries
bayestestR gives a tidy summary of each parameter’s posterior distribution, including the median estimate and a 95% credible interval (the range within which we believe the true value plausibly falls, given the model and data).

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Visualizing the posterior
The plot below shows the posterior distribution for each fixed-effect coefficient - essentially, how much belief the model places on each possible effect size after seeing the data.

mcmc_plot(fit, type = "areas", variable = "^b_", regex = TRUE)




Posterior distributions of the fixed-effect coefficients.




tidybayes lets us extract the posterior draws for the effect we care most about - the difference in RT between the Same and Different location conditions (our simulated inhibition-of-return effect) - and plot its full distribution directly.

fit %>%
  spread_draws(b_LocationSame) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = b_LocationSame)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill = "#005F73") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Estimated effect of Same vs. Different location (ms)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Posterior distribution of the location effect"
  )




Posterior distribution of the Same vs. Different location effect (ms).

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Open with the claim, not the background. One short paragraph that tells the reader what the post argues, so they can decide in ten seconds whether to keep going. Assume they have not read anything else on this site.
Then the second paragraph does the setup — why the question matters, what the usual framing gets wrong. Prose runs at a 68-character measure and is justified, so paragraphs of three to six sentences sit better than very long or very short ones.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
The usual framing
Use ## for sections. Each one gets a hairline rule above it, which is what gives a long post its rhythm — so use them generously, roughly every three or four paragraphs, and give them real titles rather than “Background” or “Discussion”.
Inline formatting works as you’d expect: emphasis, strong, inline code, and a link. A footnote goes like this1 and collects at the bottom of the post.

A pull quote is a hairline on the left and larger type. Use one when a sentence is worth stopping on — not to break up text you think is boring.


A sub-point
### is available for a level below, though most posts don’t need it.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Something worth flagging






NoteA note to one side



Callouts render as a hairline box with an accent rule on the left. .callout-note is the neutral one; .callout-warning, .callout-important and .callout-tip all work and look the same in this theme. Good for a methodological caveat or an aside that would derail the paragraph.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Showing your work
If the post needs numbers, write the chunk and let it run — the output is framed automatically and the code block keeps its highlighting:

# Any R works here. Keep chunks short enough to read on screen.
summary(cars$speed)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    4.0    12.0    15.0    15.4    19.0    25.0 


Plots get a caption and are matted like a photograph. fig-cap writes the caption; fig-alt is the screen-reader description and is worth filling in:

plot(cars$speed, cars$dist,
     pch = 16, col = "#4b7a55",
     xlab = "Speed (mph)", ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)")







Figure 1: Figure 1. Stopping distance against speed, from the built-in cars data.





Refer to it in the text as Figure 1 and Quarto numbers and links it for you.
An ordinary image, if you want one without R:



A caption sits under the plate, left-aligned.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Closing
Land the argument. One paragraph, no summary of what you just said — say the thing you were building toward, or the question you’re leaving open.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
How to use this file
Copy the whole template-post/ folder, rename it to a slug (blog/detection-is-the-wrong-test/), replace the front matter and the body, and delete this last section. The folder name becomes the URL. Keep each post’s images inside its own folder so a post stays self-contained.

title: What we lose when we stop being able to tell
text:
Footnotes


Footnotes are good for the caveat you don’t want in the main sentence.↩︎

title: Example Post: Blogging Template
text: This page is a working template, not a real post - it exists to show the correct pattern for writing one. Everything below demonstrates something worth copying.

title: Example Post: Blogging Template
text:
Heading Structure
Quarto turns the title: field above into the page’s main heading automatically, so headings inside the post body should start one level down, at ## (not # - using # here would create a second, duplicate top-level heading).

## (H2) marks a major section of the post, like this one.
### (H3) marks a subsection within it, like the one directly below.

Quarto builds the page’s table of contents from these headings, so keeping them in order (H2 before H3, no skipped levels) keeps the TOC sensible.

A Subsection Example
This is what a subsection looks like - one level below the section it belongs to.

title: Example Post: Blogging Template
text:
Code Chunks
Code chunks use three backticks and curly braces naming the language, e.g. ```{r} or ```{python}. The #| lines at the top of a chunk are chunk options - settings for that one chunk only. Two of the most useful:

echo - whether the code itself is shown on the page (true) or hidden, showing only its output (false).
eval - whether the code actually runs when the site is rendered (true), or is just displayed as text without being executed (false). Useful for showing code that depends on something not guaranteed to be available at render time - a package, an API key, a large dataset - without breaking the build.


R example
This site’s other R pages (the LinkedIn games and Bayesian analysis projects) both use this same R engine, so this is the more “native” language for this site.

mean(c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42))

[1] 18




Python example
Python chunks work the same way, through the same R-based engine (via a package called reticulate that lets R call out to Python) - as long as the post’s front matter does not add a jupyter: python3 line. Setting eval: false here on purpose, just to demonstrate the option; remove it in a real post if you want the code to actually run.

import statistics
statistics.mean([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42])

text: About

title: A researcher who’s following the machines.
text:
Who I am


I’m a PhD researcher in Psychology at the University of Hull, funded by the White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership. My work sits at the intersection of human cognition and artificial intelligence — how our minds adapt, resist and evolve as AI becomes harder to tell apart from reality.
I’m also broadly interested in the wider social and philosophical fallout of an AI-saturated world — from AI-generated misinformation to what “real” and “fake” even mean anymore. Most of that thinking ends up on the blog.

title: A researcher who’s following the machines.
text:
My research


PhD · 2025 — Joint action with an artificial partner
Does the social Inhibition of Return (sIOR) effect survive when the other actor in the task is an artificial rather than a person?


MSc · 2024 Distinction The ethics of seeing
How people judge the authenticity of AI-altered images, and how context moderates what we find acceptable. 700+ participants; multilevel SEM.

My full academic history is on my CV.

title: Hello! I’m Chin Wei.
text:
I study what shifts in cognition when the other actor in the task is an artificial one.
PhD researcher in psychology at the University of Hull, funded by the White Rose DTP. How people extend — and withdraw — agency toward artificial agents, and what that does to social cognition.

title: Hello! I’m Chin Wei.
text:
Research
Social inhibition of return in human–agent joint action, and how people judge the authenticity of AI-altered images. Preregistered experiments, SEM, Bayesian estimation.
